title: Daily learning
tomorrow: the 'what went wrong' list is way longer than the good one. now what?

lines: WHAT DO YOU DO WITH WAITING?
cards: The email opens with "Thank you for your patience," which is never a great sign. Not accepted. Not rejected.
Deferred: we'll decide later. Amira reads it twice at the counter between orders. Her counselor texts: use the time.
And what she actually wants is a week of shows under a blanket. A deferral is a strange kind of waiting, because nothing you do changes the date. So what does a person do with it?
Islam's answer is small, and it starts with a single word.

teach.b: The word is iqra: read. Tradition says it was the first word revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, in a cave, alone, and in Pickthall's words the verse runs: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth."
A faith whose scripture opens on read treats learning as worship, not as a pre-college requirement.
In a report in Ibn Majah, the Prophet says seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim. Not on scholars only; on every one.
And in Sahih Muslim: whoever takes a path to seek knowledge, God makes easy for them a path to Paradise. Even the Prophet is told in the Qur'an to ask for more of it.
In Pickthall's words: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." So here's what the tradition hands someone stuck in a deferral. The waiting isn't wasted if something is being learned in it.
Not a five-hour study plan to prove a point. That burns out by Thursday, the way the whole-Qur'an plan nearly did. A small daily amount, the way a wird is small.
This lesson's number is ten minutes. That's not a hadith; it's just a size anyone can keep. Ten minutes of a tafsir, a history, a language, a skill.
And then the shows, guilt-free. The date doesn't move. The person waiting for it does.

how: Muslims pursue daily learning through a short lesson after a prayer, a tafsir circle at the mosque, an online class, or reading with a teacher; the prayer 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge' (20:114) is one that some students say before study.

o: years of full-time study needed to become a scholar
memorizing the whole Qur'an before learning anything else
a small amount of learning every day, done as worship

games.q: learning as worship — tap the pairs.
p: made easy: a path to Paradise

s: a hadith says seeking knowledge is only for scholars
in Ibn Majah, it's an obligation on every Muslim.
the Qur'an tells the Prophet himself to ask for more knowledge
'My Lord! Increase me in knowledge,' in Pickthall's words.
'ten minutes a day' comes from a hadith
it's this lesson's size, chosen because anyone can keep it; the hadith ask for constancy, not a number.

games.q: at dinner your little brother asks why the Qur'an says 'read' to a man who, he heard, couldn't read. you don't know. what fits today?
o: tell him that's a question for when he's older.
say 'i don't know. let's find out together,' and look with a teacher's help.
give the answer that sounds most likely so he isn't confused.
games.why: seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim, kids included, and the Prophet himself asks for more. not knowing is the start of the path, not a failure.

practice: On a piece of paper, write one question you'd honestly like answered: about your faith, about the world, about anything. Write it by hand, and underline the word you understand least.
Then sit with the question, without looking anything up yet.

wordCard.voice: Daily learning: a small amount of learning every day, treated as worship, in a faith whose first revealed word, tradition says, was read.

orig.note: Arabic: read, or recite; the word that opens surah 96.

carryVoice: Here's your line: ten minutes, and then the blanket. See you at the end of the day.
